title: wind, breath and fire
hookLine: the third name nobody explained, and what speaking in tongues is
tomorrow: a library that tells one story

cards: Of the three names, Father and Son come with pictures. The Holy Spirit can feel like the one nobody explained. Maybe you saw people speaking in tongues at a friend's church and wondered what was happening.
Maybe you wondered why it never happened to you. The words underneath are plainer than you'd think: breath, and wind.

teach.b: In Hebrew the word is ruach; in Greek, pneuma. Both mean breath, wind and spirit, all at once. On the Bible's first page, the spirit of God, or the wind of God, moves over the waters.
In John's Gospel, the risen Jesus breathes on his friends and says: receive the Holy Spirit.
Jesus calls the Spirit the Paraclete: the one called alongside you. A helper, an advocate, someone in your corner. Then fire.

Fifty days after Passover, at the festival of Pentecost, his friends hear a sound like a rushing wind, something like flames rests on each of them, and they speak in languages the visiting crowd can understand.
Speaking in tongues today is understood in different ways. Pentecostal and charismatic churches treasure it as a living gift, often as a way of praying.
Some churches believe that gift belonged mainly to the first generation; many others are open to it but rarely practice it.
And Paul, writing to a church that prized it, asks: "do all speak with tongues?" He expects the answer no. His list of what the Spirit grows is quieter: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness.

how: Christians pray to and through the Holy Spirit and celebrate Pentecost fifty days after Easter; in Pentecostal and charismatic churches, speaking in tongues, healing prayer and prophecy are part of worship, while many other churches pray more quietly for the Spirit's gifts and fruit.

games.q: what's inside the name — tap the pairs.

s: in Hebrew and Greek, spirit and breath are the same word
ruach in Hebrew, pneuma in Greek: breath, wind, spirit.
every church practices speaking in tongues
Pentecostal and charismatic churches do; many others rarely or never do.
Pentecost comes fifty days after Passover
the name comes from the Greek for fiftieth.

games.q: Jesus's friends are together at Pentecost. a sound like a rushing wind fills the house. what happens next?
o: something like flames rests on each of them, and they speak in languages the crowd understands.
games.why: wind, then fire, then words every visitor could understand. it's often called the birthday of the church.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, just notice the air: in, and out. On the second, remember that in the old languages, breath and spirit are one word.
On the third, breathe slowly, and let it be enough.

wordCard.voice: The Holy Spirit. Ruach, pneuma: breath, wind, spirit, the helper called alongside. Sixth word.

orig.note: Hebrew: breath, wind, spirit. Greek holds the same three in one word: pneuma.

carryVoice: Your line: closer than your own breath. In the old languages, it's the same word. See you on day seven.
